title: Ta med eller ha med — bringing and having something with you
goal: Distinguish causing accompaniment from already having something with you.

objectives.statement: Distinguish causing accompaniment from already having something with you.

spans.value: Nora and Emil are going to spend the weekend at Nora’s family cabin. Nora is already on the bus to the station when Emil calls her.
Jeg går hjemmefra om ti minutter. Skal jeg ta med noe mat?

blocks.translation: I’m leaving home in ten minutes. Shall I bring some food?

spans.value: Ja, ta med brød og ost. Det er ikke så mye mat på hytta.

blocks.translation: Yes, bring bread and cheese. There isn’t much food at the cabin.

spans.value: Greit. Har du med nøkkelen?

blocks.translation: Fine. Do you have the key with you?

spans.value: Vent litt … Nei, jeg har ikke med nøkkelen! Den ligger hjemme.

blocks.translation: Wait a moment … No, I don’t have the key with me! It’s at home.

spans.value: Da kan jeg ta den med. Hvor ligger den?

blocks.translation: Then I can bring it. Where is it?

spans.value: Den ligger på bordet i gangen. Takk! Har du med varme klær?

blocks.translation: It’s on the table in the hall. Thanks! Do you have warm clothes with you?

spans.value: Jeg har med en genser, men ikke regnjakke.

blocks.translation: I have a sweater with me, but not a rain jacket.

spans.value: Ta med regnjakka også. Det skal regne hele helga.

blocks.translation: Bring the rain jacket too. It’s going to rain all weekend.

spans.value: The conversation turns on one small but important distinction. Nora wants Emil to make several things accompany him when he leaves home: food, the key, and a rain jacket. She therefore uses
ta med
. When Emil asks what Nora already has in her possession on the journey, he uses
ha med

Both expressions can correspond to English phrases such as bring, take along, or have with you. The useful distinction is not simply between English bring and take. Instead, ask whether the sentence presents an action or an existing situation.

sections.title: Ta med: make someone or something accompany you

spans.value: Use
ta med
when a person causes an object or another person to come along from one place to another.

no.value: Jeg tar med kaffe til møtet.

en.value: I’m bringing coffee to the meeting.

spans.value: The coffee will accompany the speaker to the meeting.

en.value: Can you bring your passport?

spans.value: The listener is being asked to make sure the passport comes along.

no.value: Mari tar med sønnen sin på festen.

en.value: Mari is bringing her son to the party.

spans.value: Mari causes her son to accompany her to the party. This does not imply force; it simply presents Mari as the person arranging or enabling his presence.

sections.title: Ha med: already have someone or something with you

spans.value: Use
ha med
when the sentence describes what someone has with them in the current situation or during a journey.

en.value: I have coffee with me.

spans.value: The sentence describes the speaker’s present situation. The coffee is already with the speaker.

en.value: Do you have your passport with you?

spans.value: The question checks whether the passport is already among the things accompanying the listener.

no.value: Mari har med sønnen sin på festen.

en.value: Mari has her son with her at the party.

spans.value: Mari and her son are already there together, or the sentence views his presence as part of her current situation.
A compact way to remember the contrast is:
ta med
focuses on getting something or someone to accompany you.
ha med
focuses on having that thing or person with you.

sections.title: First checkpoint: identify action and situation

spans.value: Read the cabin dialogue again. Find every use of
ta med
and
ha med
. For each one, note whether Emil or Nora is arranging for something to come along or checking what is already with someone.

sections.title: Compare the forms in the same context

spans.value: The contrast becomes especially clear when only the expression changes.

en.value: I’m taking an umbrella with me.
I have an umbrella with me.

spans.value: The first sentence presents the decision or action of making the umbrella accompany the speaker. The second reports the speaker’s current state: the umbrella is already with them.
Consider a traveller preparing to leave:

no.value: Før jeg går, tar jeg med billetten.

en.value: Before I leave, I take the ticket with me.

spans.value: Now consider the same traveller during an inspection:

en.value: I have the ticket with me.

spans.value: The ticket may be in a pocket or bag.
Ha med
does not mean that the person is holding it in their hand. It means that it is available because it accompanied them.
The same distinction works with people:

no.value: Vi tar med Anna på kino.

en.value: We’re taking Anna with us to the cinema.

no.value: Vi har med Anna på kino.

en.value: We have Anna with us at the cinema.

spans.value: The first sentence focuses on Anna joining the trip or plan. The second presents her as already accompanying the group.
Time and setting often make the intended expression easier to choose.
Before someone leaves, speakers often discuss what to
ta med

no.value: Hva skal vi ta med på turen?

en.value: What shall we take with us on the trip?
Bring good shoes.

no.value: Jeg kan ta med litt frukt.

en.value: I can bring some fruit.

spans.value: During the trip or after arrival, speakers often check what people
har med

en.value: What do you have with you?

no.value: Vi har med mat og varme klær.

en.value: We have food and warm clothes with us.
Does anyone have a map with them?

spans.value: This before-and-after pattern is useful, but it is not an absolute grammar rule. The real distinction remains action versus existing accompaniment. You can describe a habitual action with
ta med
, and you can talk about a future state with
ha med

no.value: Jeg tar alltid med vann når jeg går på tur.

en.value: I always take water with me when I go hiking.

no.value: I morgen har jeg med matpakke på jobb.

en.value: Tomorrow I’ll have a packed lunch with me at work.

spans.value: In the first sentence, the speaker repeatedly makes water accompany them. In the second, the speaker imagines tomorrow’s situation at work and states what they will have with them.

sections.title: Second checkpoint: complete the travel sequence

spans.value: Write one appropriate expression in each gap in this short sequence:

no.value: Før Lea går til flyplassen, må hun ___ passet.

en.value: Before Lea goes to the airport, she must ___ her passport.

no.value: På flyplassen spør venninnen: ___ du ___ passet?

en.value: At the airport her friend asks: ___ you ___ your passport with you?

no.value: Lea åpner veska og sier at hun ___ passet.

en.value: Lea opens her bag and says that she ___ her passport with her.

spans.value: First, the passport must be made part of the journey; later, its presence is checked and confirmed. Your response should change expression when the situation changes, even though the object remains the same.
In everyday conversation,
ta med
often appears in requests. The speaker wants another person to bring something or someone.

no.value: Kan du ta med melk hjem?

en.value: Can you bring milk home?
Remember to bring the charger.

no.value: Ta med en venn hvis du vil.

en.value: Bring a friend if you want.

spans.value: By contrast,
ha med
often appears in checks and reports.

en.value: Do you have the charger with you?
I don’t have cash with me.
She has a friend with her.

spans.value: Notice the natural sequence:

en.value: Remember to bring your access card.
Yes, I have it with me.

spans.value: The first speaker refers to the action needed. The second confirms the resulting situation.
Using ha med for an instruction
A learner may produce:

en.value: Have the passport with you tomorrow.

spans.value: This can be understood, and Norwegian sometimes allows such wording when the intended state is strongly emphasized. However, if the ordinary purpose is to tell someone to bring the passport,
ta med
is the clearer and more natural choice:

en.value: Bring your passport tomorrow.

spans.value: The instruction concerns making sure the passport comes along.
Using ta med when checking a current situation
At the airport, this question does not normally perform the intended check:

en.value: Are you bringing the passport?

spans.value: It asks about the person’s plan or action. If you can see that the person has already arrived and want to know whether the passport is with them, ask:

en.value: Do you have your passport with you?

spans.value: Compare the contexts:

no.value: Du er fortsatt hjemme. Tar du med passet?

en.value: You’re still at home. Are you bringing your passport?

no.value: Du er på flyplassen. Har du med passet?

en.value: You’re at the airport. Do you have your passport with you?

spans.value: Translating one English verb mechanically
English bring can refer either to the action of bringing or to the result of having brought something. Norwegian often makes the distinction more explicit.

no.value: Jeg tar med kake til festen.

en.value: I’m bringing cake to the party.
I’ve brought cake. / I have cake with me.

spans.value: In the second example, English may naturally use I’ve brought, but the Norwegian sentence views the cake as already present with the speaker. This is why direct word-for-word translation is less reliable than asking whether the sentence focuses on action or state.
Rewrite each statement as a later check or report. Keep the same person and object, but move the situation from preparation to arrival.

no.value: Sander tar med dokumentene til kontoret.

en.value: Sander is bringing the documents to the office.

no.value: Vi tar med håndklær til stranda.

en.value: We’re taking towels to the beach.

no.value: Mina tar med søsteren sin på konserten.

en.value: Mina is bringing her sister to the concert.

spans.value: Then reverse the task. Turn each current report into an earlier plan or request.

en.value: Sander has the documents with him.
We have towels with us.
Mina has her sister with her.

spans.value: Your response should use
ta med
for preparation or movement and
ha med
for the resulting situation.
Emil reaches the station and finds Nora beside the bus.
Hei! Fikk du tatt med nøkkelen?

blocks.translation: Hi! Did you manage to bring the key?

spans.value: Ja, jeg har den med her.

blocks.translation: Yes, I have it with me here.

spans.value: Flott. Og regnjakka?
Den har jeg også med. Men jeg glemte osten.

blocks.translation: I have that with me too. But I forgot the cheese.

spans.value: Det går bra. Jeg har med litt mat, og vi kan handle på veien.

blocks.translation: That’s fine. I have some food with me, and we can shop on the way.

spans.value: Neste gang tar jeg med en handleliste.

blocks.translation: Next time I’ll bring a shopping list.

spans.value: The key first appears as something Emil must
ta med
from Nora’s home. At the station, he can say that he
har den med
because the action has produced a new situation: the key is now with him. His final sentence returns to
ta med
because he is talking about a future action.
Imagine three moments in one day: preparing for a picnic, meeting at the bus stop, and arriving at the park. Write short Norwegian sentences that do the following:

items.value: Before departure, state that one person will bring food.
At the bus stop, check whether another person has a blanket with them.
At the park, report that someone has two friends with them.
While discussing the next picnic, ask someone to bring a ball.

spans.value: Keep each sentence focused on whether accompaniment is being caused or already exists. Your responses should use the same distinction consistently across objects and people.
Without looking back, write two connected Norwegian sentences about one object: first arrange for it to accompany someone, then confirm that the person has it with them.

prompt.value: Sort the lines by whether they are about bringing someone or something along, or having it with you.

explanation.value: «Ta med» beskriver handlingen der noe blir med. «Ha med» forteller at noe allerede er med.

Sjekke eller si at noe allerede er med

items.text: Skal jeg ta med noe mat?
Da kan jeg ta den med.

prompt.value: Fill in the three blanks in the airport dialogue.

explanation.value: I det første feltet beskriver verbet at passet blir tatt med fra ett sted til et annet. I de to siste feltene spør og forteller man om passet allerede er med.

spans.value: «Når jeg drar hjemmefra, må jeg
passet fra bordet til flyplassen.» Ida: «Nå som vi står ved sikkerhetskontrollen,
passet med deg?» Lea: «Ja, jeg
passet i vesken.»

text.value: «Når jeg drar hjemmefra, må jeg ___ passet fra bordet til flyplassen.»
«Nå som vi står ved sikkerhetskontrollen, ___ passet med deg?»

prompt.value: Rewrite the six details as short sentences in Norwegian. Use «ha med» for what people have with them now, and «ta med» for what they plan to bring.

explanation.value: De tre første setningene forteller hva personene har med seg nå. De tre siste beskriver noe de planlegger å ta med. Begge plasseringene av «med» kan være naturlige på norsk.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate six-facts, viewpoint-contrast, norwegian. Accept natural Bokmål variants that preserve each fact and meaning, including «Sander har med dokumentene» and «Sander har dokumentene med»; do not require a single position for med.

criteria.instruction: Preserves all six facts: Sander has the documents; we have towels; Mina has her sister with her; Sander plans to take the documents to the office; we plan to take towels to the beach; Mina plans to take her sister to the concert.
Uses ha med to report what is currently with someone in the first three sentences, and ta med for planned actions in the last three; accept natural placement of med before or after the object.
The sentences are understandable, natural Bokmål.

text.value: «Før avreise sørger Sander for at dokumentene blir med til kontoret.»
«Vi sørger for at håndklærne blir med til stranda.»
«Jeg sørger for at søsteren min blir med på konserten.»

prompt.value: Write a message to your teacher about the picnic day. Ali made sure the food was brought along before they left. At the bus stop, Nora checked whether Liv had a blanket with her. In the park, Mina had two friends with her. For the next picnic, Nora asked Ali to make sure a ball is brought along. Use both «ta med» and «ha med» naturally in the message.

explanation.value: Før avreise handler det om å sørge for at noe blir med. Senere spør man om noe allerede er med eller forteller at det er det.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate criteria message-purpose, supplied-facts, norwegian-text, action-form, and state-form as gating criteria. Record the observation criteria diagnostically, but do not fail a response based on them. The prompt requests both taught expressions, so require them for the two form criteria.

criteria.instruction: Writes a coherent message to the teacher that reports the planning and course of the picnic day.
Communicates all four supplied facts without materially changing who acts, what accompanies them, or when each event occurs.
Writes the message in understandable Norwegian.
Uses a natural ta med form for both actions that arrange accompaniment.
Uses a natural ha med form for the bus-stop check and park report.
Observation only: note whether the taught ta med form appears; do not fail a natural equivalent.
Observation only: note whether the taught ha med form appears; do not fail a natural equivalent.

prompt.value: You and Erik are by the car before going for a walk. Write a short message asking him to bring the umbrella from the car and saying that you want to have it with you on the walk. Use both «ta med» and «ha med».

explanation.value: Begge setningene gjelder før turen. Den første ber om at paraplyen blir tatt med, og den andre sier at dere skal ha den med på turen.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate criteria recipient-and-purpose, single-setting, same-object, norwegian-text, action-form, and state-form as gating criteria. The prompt requests both taught expressions, so require them for the two form criteria while accepting natural inflection and placement variants.

criteria.instruction: Addresses Erik with one coherent message before the walk, asking him to bring the umbrella from the car and expressing that it is wanted on the walk.
Both clauses make sense in the same setting and at the same time, before the walk begins.
Both clauses concern the same umbrella.
Writes the message in understandable Norwegian.
Uses a natural ta med form to ask Erik to bring the umbrella from the car.
Uses a natural ha med form to say that they want the umbrella with them on the walk.

prompt.value: You are packing sunglasses for a mountain trip. Write one sentence saying that you will make sure to bring them. Use «ta med» in the correct form.

explanation.value: «Ta med» beskriver handlingen der solbrillene blir pakket til turen.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate only criterion action-expression. Accept a grammatical sentence using the taught expression for the planned action of bringing the sunglasses along, and add no other gating requirement.

criteria.instruction: Uses ta med to express the planned action of bringing the sunglasses along.

prompt.value: You are at the cabin, and the flashlight is already in your backpack. Write one sentence saying that you have it with you on the hike. Use «ha med» in the correct form.

explanation.value: «Ha med» forteller at lommelykten allerede er med på turen.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate only criterion state-expression. Accept a grammatical sentence using the taught expression for the flashlight already being with the speaker, and add no other gating requirement.

criteria.instruction: Uses ha med to report that the flashlight is already with the speaker.
